Results
In all study 2 (and study 3) analyses, covariates and dem-
ographics had no effect. Their inclusion in analyses does
not change any conclusion. We drop them in what we report
below.
Manipulation Check.
Participants rated themselves to
have made less progress in the ﬁrst game when they were
in the goal far (M p 23.48%) than goal near condition (M
p 74.67%; F(1, 40) = 100.60, = < .01, h2 p .716).
Willingness to Be Interrupted Now.
A logistic regression
analysis showed that more people chose to play the 5-minute
iPad game now when they were far from the goal rather
than near (85.7% vs. 47.6%; x2(1) = 6.14, = < .05, f p
.404). People preferred to delay interruption when closer to
goal completion even when doing so caused delay in overall
goal completion. We found no differences in spare time
perceptions or ratings of bother at the interruption. We return
to these ﬁndings in “Meta-Analysis of Results of Studies 1
through 4.”
Discussion
These results replicated an earlier study (N p 92) with
minor variations. There, 51% of those interrupted early in
game 1, and 26% of those interrupted later chose to do the
interrupting game now (x2(1) = 6.71, = = .01). Game 1
was not paused if the participant chose to be interrupted
now, leaving a switching cost alternative account. Studies
2 and 3 paused the game so that no progress could be lost,

Data source. In this analysis we compared the effects based on 
the EEO data set with all other effects. The mean effects dif-
fered under both the fixed-effects model, QBetween(1) = 14.59, p = 
.0001, and the mixed model, z = 2.17, p = .03. Data source 
explained nearly half of the between-studies variation in the 
correlations (R2Meta = .46). The four EEO effects were not 
homogeneous, as our initial analyses revealed. However, effects 
not based on EEO data were homogeneous, QWithin(12) = 9.20, 
p = .69,13 suggesting that the non-EEO effects arose from one 
population. The weighted overall mean for the 13 non-EEO 
correlations was .04 (SE = .026), with a 95% CI from –.01 to 
.09, compared with a mean of .17 for the 4 EEO effects (SE = 
.054; 95% CI from .06 to .27). Thus all correlations except 
those from the EEO study showed no relationship of teachers’ 
verbal ability to any outcome.
